slides.0.title: Style in depth: oxidative vs reductive, ageing and dosage
slides.0.subtitle: Same region, different styles from winemaking decisions
slides.1.title: Reductive and oxidative: a spectrum
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The reductive approach
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Stainless steel, low oxygen and careful SO₂ protect primary fruit and acidity: a clean, bright style of citrus and green apple that is ready earlier, at the cost of some textural complexity
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The oxidative approach
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Fermenting or maturing in oak (often old), contact with lees and less SO₂ give nutty, baked-apple and honeyed notes already at base-wine stage, with broader texture and more ageing potential. Oak barrels are allowed but wood chips are banned (Level 2)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: It is not either/or
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Most houses mix the two: some base wines in barrel, some in tank, with proportions set at blending. “Oxidative” is a stylistic tendency, not a quality grade or a legal category
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Tasting clues
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Reductive: lemon, green apple, white blossom, bright acidity. Oxidative: nuts, baked apple, honey, cream, deeper colour and broader palate. Ageing also brings nuts and caramel, so separate “winemaking oxidation” from “age” by asking whether the fruit is still fresh underneath
slides.1.content: Separate “style choice” from “quality”: it keeps preference from being written up as fact.
slides.2.title: MLF, vessels and reserve wine
slides.2.highlights.0.title: MLF: keep or drop the malic acid
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Comité Champagne describes MLF as optional: with it the wine is rounder and softer in acid; without it malic acid stays and the wine is sharper. In warm, low-acid years skipping MLF is a tool to keep acidity, and some houses make “no MLF” a style signature
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Choice of vessel
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Stainless steel (pure, controllable), old oak (texture, micro-oxygenation); other vessels such as concrete eggs or amphorae are not forbidden by the specification but are the house’s choice. Individual producers’ practices are not listed here (not verified item by item)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Reserve wine: the stabiliser of NV style
slides.2.highlights.2.content: NV aims for a consistent house style: the current year brings freshness and reserve wine brings maturity and complexity (Comité Champagne). Each producer may hold up to 10,000 kg/ha in reserve, and reserve wine cannot carry a vintage (Level 2). The share of reserve wine is each house’s decision and varies, so no figure is given here
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Perpetual reserve and climate change
slides.2.highlights.3.content: A perpetual reserve is topped up with new wine each year and part is drawn off, making the reserve a multi-vintage blend; it is a house choice (Level 2). With climate change reserves matter more: older, more acidic base wines can make up for missing acidity in warm years, but NV style then depends more heavily on stock and cellar management
slides.2.content: The point of reserve wine is consistency across years: it is both a stylistic tool and a financial and supply buffer (revisited in ch-l3-5).
slides.3.title: Lees ageing, disgorgement and post-disgorgement age
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The legal minimum is only a starting point
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Specification: from tirage, NV ≥ 15 months and Vintage ≥ 36 months, with disgorgement not before 12 months (Level 2). The Comité notes that most producers age beyond the minimum; the longer the ageing, the more marked the autolytic notes (a trend, not a hard number)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Autolysis: the flavour shift
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Compounds released by dead yeast bring brioche, toast and almond and make the mousse finer and the texture silkier (Level 2). In tasting, autolytic aromas (bread, biscuit, cream) are the first clue to the length of lees ageing
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Disgorgement date and post-disgorgement age
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The INAO labelling clauses contain no mandatory disgorgement date, though some producers print one voluntarily. It lets you separate time on lees (protected by the lees) from time after disgorgement (no lees; a different evolution influenced by closure and dosage). They are not the same thing
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Ageing potential and tertiary aromas
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Vintage and prestige wines usually age longer, with tertiary notes such as dried fruit, honey, mushroom and caramel; the test of quality is whether acidity and tension remain. “Prestige” is a market term with no legal definition (Level 2)
slides.3.content: Exam language: lees ageing (autolysis) first, post-disgorgement age second, overall balance last.
slides.4.title: Dosage: sweetness, balance and the zero-dosage trend
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Dosage is more than “adding sugar”
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Dosage is the liqueur d’expédition (wine plus sugar) added after disgorgement to balance acidity, shape texture and influence ageing. Categories: Brut Nature <3, Extra Brut 0–6, Brut <12, Extra Dry 12–17, Sec 17–32, Demi-Sec 32–50, Doux >50 g/L, with ±3 g/L tolerance (Level 2)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: What Brut Nature means
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Brut Nature means residual sugar below 3 g/L with no added sugar (DGCCRF label guide). It demands ripe fruit, rounded acidity and long ageing, otherwise the wine feels angular; the same wine will not suit zero dosage in every vintage
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Should dosage fall as the climate warms?
slides.4.highlights.2.content: For lower dosage: riper fruit and richer texture need less sugar to round them off. Against a blanket cut: acidity is falling too, some years still need dosage to balance remaining acid, and very low dosage can expose bitterness and leanness. This is a core MW question; ch-l3-6 gives a framework
slides.4.highlights.3.title: The single-plot, single-year trend
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Some producers now stress lieu-dit, clos, single-village or single-vintage cuvées, using terroir transparency as a counterpoint to the blending tradition. This is a market and style trend, not an extra tier inside the AOC, and quality still depends on the plot and the producer
slides.4.content: In essays do not stop at “sweet or dry”: dosage affects acidity, texture, ageing and consumer positioning at once.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
What does the INAO specification say about oak in base-wine fermentation?
A. Both barrels and wood chips are allowed
B. Oak barrels may be used but wood chips are banned
Barrels are allowed but wood chips (morceaux de bois) are prohibited.
C. Residual sugar below 3 g/L with no added sugar
Brut Nature is below 3 g/L with no added sugar; Extra Dry is 12–17 and Doux above 50 g/L.
In a warm, low-acid year, what is the main purpose of skipping MLF?
C. To make the wine sweeter
D. To keep malic acid and preserve acidity and tension
MLF converts sharp malic acid to softer lactic acid; skipping it keeps the acidity (Comité Champagne).
